function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
The user wants temperature forecast for next week in New York City. We need to use the tool `requests_get` to fetch weather data from Open-Meteo API.

We have to provide coordinates for NYC: latitude ~40.7128°N, longitude -74.0060°W. Use open-meteo.com API? Let's check typical usage:

Open-Meteo API example:
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=52.52&longitude=13.41&hourly=temperature_2m

But we want weekly forecast maybe daily average temperatures. For next week, we can get daily forecasts for next 7 days. So query params: latitude=40.7128, longitude=-74.0060, hourly/daily variables like temperature_2m_max/min etc. But easier: daily variable "temperature_2m_mean". Or "temperature_2m_min", "max".

Let's choose daily max and min. Provide start_date and end_date as needed. Next week starting tomorrow? Suppose today is unknown but we can ask them to specify dates. However they just asked "next week." We'll assume upcoming Monday through Sunday relative to current day. But we don't know today's date. Could approximate using system date via python? Not possible here. Instead we could call API without specifying dates so returns future forecast including next week automatically. Then parse results accordingly.

We'll make an API call with daily variables: temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min. Also set timezone parameter to America/New_York.

So we'll do:

URL: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast

Params: 
latitude=40.7128
longitude=-74.0060
daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min
timezone=Africa/Cairo?? Actually timezone param expects IANA tz e.g., America/New_York.

Also optionally add "start_date" and "end_date"? Might not necessary if omitted defaults to now+days? According to docs, you can omit start/end and will return forecast for next 30 days. Good enough.

Thus we call the function.

After retrieving JSON, we extract daily arrays for next 7 days. Show table of date, high temp, low temp.

Ok let's proceed.
